summary: Steel Dome Lookout on Second Dome near Dawson City, staffed each summer; build year conflicts (1963 vs 1965) and the height is given as both 70 m and 70 ft.

facts.design: Steel structure anchored by guy wires, with an octagonal cupola painted red and white; a modest log cabin with a front porch stands beside it

staffing.status: Staffed each fire season (May to August) by lookout Markus Lenzin

access.note: A visitor listing says the tower was locked partway up. No official source describes whether the public may climb it.

visit.trail_note: A steep gravel road branches off Dome Road to the site.

events.note: Canada's Fire Lookouts, as quoted by ExploreNorth, dates the Dome tower in Dawson City to 1963. The Moyles article says it was built as early as 1965.
Staffed regardless of fire risk during the 2014 season, one of six of the Yukon's nine fire towers.
Markus Lenzin has kept vigil at the Dawson Lookout for the past 15 summers, per the 2024 article.
On June 26 Lenzin caught the Moosehide Creek Fire, which ignited after dry lightning struck a tree less than seven kilometres from the tower.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Canada's Fire Lookouts (via ExploreNorth) gives 1963; the Moyles article says built as early as 1965 and in the mid-to-late 1960s. The story reports both and does not pick one.
The Moyles article gives 70 metres in a photo caption and 70 feet in its text. Both are reported in the story; no height_m is recorded.

notes_for_editor: The brief's name Dome Lookout appears in the Canada Lookouts index as DOME (AKA SECOND DOME OR FIRE DOME); the 2024 Moyles article calls it Dawson Lookout. The brief's agency (Yukon Wildland Fire Management) is not used verbatim: the Moyles article says Yukon Wildfire Management, and ExploreNorth uses Wildland Fire for a different tower; left for the editor to decide. The Yukon Fire History Atlas returned 403 and was not read. The ehcanadatravel listing says the tower is 200 feet tall, which conflicts with both other height figures; it is not used. The Moyles article spells the 2024 fire Moosehide Creek in the main text and Moosehead Creek in one quoted line; the story uses Moosehide. A recent-visit post-script in the Moyles article has no date. Read budget: about 6 page reads and 1 search.
